papers.title: PROSPER: LLMs as Sparse Retrievers for First-Stage Product Search
papers.authors: Hongru Song, Yu-An Liu, Ruqing Zhang, Jiafeng Guo, Maarten de Rijke, Sen Li, Wenjun Peng, Fuyu Lv, Xueqi Cheng
papers.abstract: Product search is a crucial component of large-scale e-commerce platforms, where first-stage retrieval should achieve high recall while ensuring efficient online deployment. Sparse retrieval remains attractive for this setting due to its interpretability and deployability, yet it suffers from severe vocabulary mismatch challenges, especially for short queries and product titles. Large language models (LLMs) offer strong semantic capabilities, but directly applying them to sparse retrieval in product search introduces new challenges: (i) semantic expansion may distort critical literal signals such as brand names and model identifiers; and (ii) learning meaningful sparse representations is difficult in the high-dimensional vocabulary space induced by LLMs.To address these challenges, we propose PROSPER, a framework that uses LLMs as sparse retrievers for product search while explicitly preserving lexical fidelity. PROSPER combines (i) a literal residual network that alleviates lexical expansion hallucination by reinforcing underweighted literal terms through a residual compensation mechanism; and (ii) a lexical focusing window that uses top-k selection for rapid early sparsification and effective training initialization. Extensive offline evaluations and large-scale online A/B tests demonstrate that PROSPER consistently improves over existing sparse retrievers, and provides revenue gains for industrial hybrid retrieval systems.
company: University of Chinese Academy of Sciences
papers.summary: First-stage product search has to reach high recall and still be easy to deploy. Sparse retrieval is interpretable and practical, but short queries and titles often miss each other in the vocabulary; using an LLM as a sparse retriever can also wash out literal signals such as brand names and model identifiers. The new method adds a residual to restore underweighted literal terms and uses a top-k window to sparsify the representation early. On the Multi-CPR e-commerce set, Hit@1000 is 10.2 points above BM25 and also ahead of SPLADE-v2. In a large-scale online A/B test, net GMV rose 1.60%, showing a revenue gain for an industrial hybrid retriever.

papers.title: SupportChain: Trace-Calibrated Aggregation of Quote-Grounded Reasoning Chains for Multi-Hop RAG with Small Readers
papers.abstract: Strong results in multi-hop retrieval-augmented question answering come from graph indexes read by models of 70B parameters or more, and building such an index calls a large language model over the whole corpus. We present SupportChain, which splits a question into hops, binds each hop's answer to a sentence quoted from a retrieved passage, estimates how reliable each execution is from its own trace, and merges several executions by the support of their answers, the pooled reliability of the executions that agree, stopping once support is high enough. With a 9B reader under the HippoRAG~2 protocol, SupportChain reaches 63.0 F1 on MuSiQue, above the best earlier result of 59.2, which used a 20B reader. With the same reader and embedder, it is significantly better than HippoRAG~2 on all five datasets, by up to 17.2 F1, and it builds no index. Merging by support is significantly better than majority voting, and than letting the reader choose among the candidates, on three of the five datasets and level with both on the other two. The reliability model needs only 100 answered training questions.
papers.summary: Strong multi-hop retrieval QA often comes from graph indexes read by very large models, and building such an index means running a language model over the whole corpus. The new method splits a question into hops, binds each hop's answer to a sentence quoted from a retrieved passage, estimates reliability from the execution trace, and merges runs by the support of their answers and the pooled reliability of those that agree. With a smaller 9B reader it reaches 63.0 F1 on MuSiQue, above the previous best of 59.2 from a 20B reader. With the same reader and embedder, it is significantly better than HippoRAG 2 on all five datasets, by up to 17.2 F1, and it builds no index.

papers.title: Pixel as the Common Language: Unified Multimodal Embedding via Visual Rendering
papers.authors: Xu Yuan, Pangjing Wu, Wenqi Fan, Qing Li
papers.abstract: Multimodal embedding models map heterogeneous inputs into a shared representation space, yet text-only, image-only, and composed inputs are still presented in distinct formats and follow different routes through the model. This fragmentation prevents heterogeneous tasks from jointly optimizing the same end-to-end encoding process, limiting supervision transfer across input configurations. To address this issue, we propose unification before encoding and instantiate this paradigm in RenderEmbed. The framework uses Visual Substrate Rendering to convert heterogeneous inputs into a common visual substrate for encoding with a VLM. From the resulting visual tokens, Progressive Hierarchical Anchor Encoding produces compact retrieval representations by interleaving learnable anchors and fusing their states across layers, retaining broad context and fine-grained cues. Interventional Rendering Learning trains these representations to remain sensitive to content changes and stable across rendering variations through complementary semantic and rendering interventions. Extensive experiments on MMEB and ViDoRe v2, spanning diverse retrieval tasks, show that RenderEmbed outperforms prior state-of-the-art models at the same scale and exhibits strong out-of-domain generalization. Compared with MetaEmbed, RenderEmbed improves MMEB Overall Precision@1 by 1.7 points, with a larger 2.1-point gain on out-of-domain tasks. Transfer and scaling analyses further show that a shared visual pathway enables more effective learning from heterogeneous supervision.
papers.summary: Multimodal embedding models usually send text-only, image-only, and composed inputs through different formats and routes, so heterogeneous tasks cannot easily share one end-to-end encoder. The new framework first renders those inputs onto a shared visual substrate, then fuses learnable anchors across layers into a compact retrieval vector, and uses interventions on content and rendering so the representation stays sensitive to content changes and stable across rendering variations. On MMEB and ViDoRe v2, it outperforms prior models at the same scale and generalizes more strongly out of domain. Compared with MetaEmbed, MMEB overall Precision@1 rises 1.7 points, with a 2.1-point gain on out-of-domain tasks.

papers.title: S$^2$LMR: Supervised Sequential Long-Context Multi-Step Retriever
papers.abstract: Multi-step retrieval over long contexts is a key capability for retrieval-augmented generation, but strong existing approaches are costly and complex to train. Supervised retrievers are far simpler and cheaper, yet they fall well behind in this setting. We show that this gap stems not from supervised training itself, but from three misalignments between training and inference: easy training negatives, noisy retrieval prefixes, and position-agnostic scoring. Guided by this analysis, we introduce S$^2$LMR, a simple yet effective supervised sequential retriever that models multi-step retrieval as the evolution of an explicit textual state encoded by a single shared Transformer. On long-context reasoning, multi-hop QA, and needle-in-a-haystack benchmarks with context lengths ranging from 4K to 10M tokens, S$^2$LMR achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art methods, substantially outperforming prior supervised retrievers. Notably, it requires only $\sim$2 hours of training on a single A6000 for contexts of up to 10M tokens, while remaining robust across a wide range of hyperparameter settings.
papers.summary: Multi-step retrieval over long contexts is usually expensive and complex to train, and simpler supervised retrievers lag far behind. The gap is not supervised training itself, but a mismatch with inference: easy training negatives, noisy retrieval prefixes, and scores that ignore position. The new method treats multi-step retrieval as the evolution of an explicit textual state encoded by one shared Transformer. On long-context reasoning, multi-hop QA, and needle-in-a-haystack benchmarks from 4K to ten million tokens, it matches strong recent methods and substantially outperforms earlier supervised retrievers. It trains in about two hours on a single A6000 for contexts up to ten million tokens, and stays above 95% accuracy at that length.

papers.title: Make Position Uninformative: Exchangeable Self-Distillation Flattens the Lost-in-the-Middle Curve
papers.authors: Qingsen Ma, Dianyun Wang, Jiahong Liu, Irwin King
papers.abstract: Retrieval-augmented language models answer well when the relevant document comes first or last and poorly when it sits in the middle. Some fine-tuning recipes lift the middle by lowering the start. We show how training contexts teach positional bias. With a uniform answer slot and shuffled distractors, the optimal reader ignores position. Building on this result, Exchangeable Self-Distillation (ExSD) trains a small adapter on shuffled contexts to reproduce the model's answer when it reads the answer document alone. It needs no gold answers and only a few thousand examples. On six models from 1.5B to 32B parameters, ExSD raises both average and worst-position accuracy against the frozen model, including on a held-out test split. In controlled LoRA comparisons, it significantly improves both criteria over Pos2Distill. Against CORD, mean differences are not significant, while worst-position accuracy improves significantly in the 20- and 30-document settings. ExSD also matches or beats gold-answer fine-tuning, changes behavior on other tasks far less, and transfers to unseen tasks. Head probes show greater reliance on content over position.
company: Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications
papers.summary: Retrieval-augmented language models usually answer well when the relevant document is first or last, and poorly when it sits in the middle; some fine-tuning recipes lift the middle by lowering the start. If the answer slot is uniform and distractors are shuffled, the optimal reader should ignore position. The new method trains a small adapter so the model, given shuffled contexts, reproduces the answer it gives when it reads the answer document alone, with no gold answers and only a few thousand examples. On six models from 1.5B to 32B, it raises both average and worst-position accuracy over the frozen model. Against CORD, mean differences are not significant, but worst-position accuracy improves significantly when more documents are present.

papers.title: CO-GRAFT: Attributing Reinforcement Learning Gains in Search Agents via Role-Level Policy Grafting
papers.authors: Ramraj Chandradevan, Sayontan Ghosh, Vinoth Selvendran
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) improves large language model search agents by up to 32 exact-match (EM) points over their pre-RL initializations, yet overall accuracy gains do not identify which underlying functional capabilities improve or interact during training. We introduce CO-GRAFT, a reward-agnostic interventional attribution framework in which an RL-trained agent and its pre-RL initialization jointly generate a single trajectory under closed-loop execution with live retrieval. Each policy controls a mutually exclusive subset of four functional roles: intermediate reasoning, search-or-answer decision, search query generation, and final answer extraction. Evaluating all 2^4=16 role assignments without modifying weights or retraining defines a cooperative game whose Shapley values decompose the total RL gain across roles, while M"obius interaction terms distinguish standalone role improvements from multi-role coupling. Applying CO-GRAFT to Search-R1 agents across Qwen2.5 and Llama-3.2 models (spanning two sizes, base and instruction-tuned initializations, GRPO and PPO optimizers, and NQ and HotpotQA datasets), we show that query generation never exceeds 15% of the total gain; instead, gains are governed by pre-RL answer validity, search retention, model scale, and fixed task-level search budgets, shifting credit from reasoning toward answer extraction in larger or well-formatted answer response checkpoints while smaller base models rely on reasoning--decision coupling.
papers.summary: Reinforcement learning can raise a search agent's exact-match score by up to 32 points over its pre-training initialization, but the overall gain does not say which capabilities actually improved. The new method lets the RL-trained agent and its initialization jointly run one live-retrieval trajectory, each controlling a subset of four roles: intermediate reasoning, the search-or-answer decision, query generation, and final answer extraction, then decomposes the total gain across those roles. Across several models and datasets, query generation never accounts for more than 15% of the total gain. What matters instead is whether pre-training answers were already valid, whether search is retained, model scale, and the task's fixed search budget.

papers.title: DM-Lab at TREC 2026 RAG: Multi-Query Retrieval, Ensemble Judging, and Claim-Pack Generation
papers.authors: Elyas Irankhah, Muhammad Arif, Sreeraj Ramachandran, Samah Fodeh-Jarad
papers.abstract: We present DM-Lab-RAG-2026, a framework developed for the TREC 2026 Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) track. The framework integrates large-scale evidence retrieval and citation-grounded answer generation over the 553-million-document ClimbMix-400B corpus. The retrieval architecture combines multi-query BM25, reciprocal rank fusion, ensemble relevance assessment, listwise reranking, and adaptive retrieval depth. The generation pipeline employs a claim-first strategy to extract evidence-linked atomic claims, construct cited responses, and verify source support. Across 22 development topics, the retrieval system achieved a mean nDCG@30 of 0.604. In the official evaluation, it attained a set precision of 0.455 and a manual nugget gain of 0.910. Additional experiments examine the influence of reranking, evidence selection, and citation verification on system performance. The evaluation demonstrates the potential of diversified lexical retrieval and language-model-based relevance assessment for large-scale evidence discovery. It further identifies evidence preservation and structured answer construction as key considerations for reliable RAG. This work provides a reproducible framework for investigating retrieval effectiveness and evidence-grounded generation.
papers.summary: Retrieval-augmented generation over hundreds of millions of documents has to find the evidence and keep every claim tied to a source. This TREC system gathers evidence with multi-query lexical retrieval, reciprocal rank fusion, ensemble relevance judging, and listwise reranking, then extracts citation-linked atomic claims before writing a verifiable answer. Across 22 development topics, retrieval reached a mean nDCG@30 of 0.604. In the official evaluation, set precision was 0.455 and manual nugget gain was 0.910. The authors also argue that reliable RAG depends on preserving evidence and on building the answer in a structured way.

papers.title: Introducing Rerank 5: precise, efficient enterprise document retrieval
papers.abstract: Both models introduce Context Focus, which pinpoints the most relevant spans of text within documents, going beyond document- or chunk-level retrieval.
papers.summary: Enterprise retrieval has to send the most relevant context to a language model, which shapes answer quality and token cost. Cohere's Rerank 5 comes in Pro and Fast tiers and adds Context Focus, so one call can mark the most relevant spans inside a document rather than only ranking whole documents or chunks. On public benchmarks, Rerank 5 Pro scores 82.2, 5.8 points above Voyage Rerank 3. Of 46 composite datasets, it ranked first on 39. The relevance scores are also calibrated across queries and domains, so teams can set one threshold for what reaches the language model.

papers.title: rerank-3 and rerank-3-lite: the next generation of Voyage rerankers
papers.abstract: Both models are trained with an updated backbone and an improved mixture of training data.
papers.summary: More queries now come from coding agents, and the documents being reranked are getting longer, so an older reranker may no longer be enough. Voyage's rerank-3 and a lighter variant upgrade the backbone and training mixture under the same API and price, with the same context length. On long-document retrieval, rerank-3 is 3.35% above the previous rerank-2.5 and 13.84% above Cohere Rerank v4.0 Pro. The lite model matches the retrieval quality of rerank-2.5 at 40% of the price. Code retrieval also improves steadily.

papers.title: ES|QL Data Federation: Elasticsearch now queries data where it lives
papers.abstract: Query Parquet, NDJSON, and CSV/TSV files in Amazon S3 directly from Elasticsearch using the same FROM syntax and Kibana. With ES|QL Data Federation, string filters run up to 115x faster, and the schema is inferred automatically, with no mapping needed.
papers.summary: A lot of logs and archives still live in object storage, and querying them often means ingesting the files first or standing up a second engine. Elastic now lets teams query Parquet, NDJSON, and CSV files in Amazon S3 with the same ES|QL syntax and Kibana, inferring the schema at query time and without a prior mapping. String filters run 40 to 115 times faster than earlier approaches through dictionary-aware vectorized evaluation. Pushing sort-and-limit into the reader is 3.6 to 4.3 times faster. The feature is in technical preview on Elastic Cloud Serverless.

scenario: Today's retrieval papers put language models into first-stage product search, and also show that a smaller reader can catch up with larger ones on multi-hop QA. Some render text and images onto one visual substrate before encoding, some treat long-context multi-step retrieval as a supervised state, and some specifically flatten the bias that answers go missing in the middle. Reinforcement-learning gains in search agents are attributed across query, decision, and answer roles, while a TREC RAG system stresses citations and packed claims. On the industry side, new rerankers start locating relevant spans inside a document, and a search engine can query files that still live in object storage.
